problemText: In 1543, the year of his death, a Polish astronomer published On the Revolutions of the Heavenly Spheres, arguing that the Sun rather than the Earth sits at the center of the planetary system. Who was he?
choices: Isaac Newton
Galileo Galilei
Nicolaus Copernicus
Johannes Kepler
hints: Match the person to the date: 1543 comes long before the telescope, the ellipse, and the law of gravitation.

problemText: Working from decades of unusually precise position measurements recorded by Tycho Brahe, Johannes Kepler concluded in 1609 that planetary orbits are ellipses rather than perfect circles. Why did this conclusion matter beyond astronomy?
choices: It showed that the Earth, not the Sun, sits at the center of the planetary system
It overturned an ancient assumption about perfectly circular heavenly motion using careful measurement rather than authority
It proved that a single force of gravitation holds the planets in their paths
It established that the Moon's surface is rough and covered with craters
hints: Ask what the old belief in perfect circles had ever been tested against — and what Kepler tested it against.

problemText: A seventeenth-century scholar insists that a claim about nature counts as knowledge only when it rests on observation and deliberate experiment that other people can repeat, and never simply because a respected ancient writer asserted it. Which position does this stance describe?
choices: Geocentrism, the view that the Earth sits at the center of the cosmos
Divine right, the claim that a ruler's authority comes directly from God
Scholasticism, the practice of settling questions about nature by reasoning from authoritative texts
Empiricism, the position that knowledge must come from observation and experiment
hints: Two choices name claims about what the world contains; only one names a standard for how a claim gets accepted.

problemText: A member of a London scientific society wrote in 1665 (paraphrased): 'We do not print a finding so that it may be admired. We print it so that any careful person in Paris or Florence may build the same apparatus, run the trial himself, and tell us plainly if we are wrong.' Which principle of the new science does this statement most directly express?
choices: A result counts as established only when independent investigators can repeat it and challenge it
Findings should be kept private until a wealthy patron approves their publication
New claims about nature should be supported by quoting respected ancient authorities
Descriptions in plain language are more trustworthy than mathematical treatment
hints: Look at who is invited to act in the passage, and what they are invited to do to the author's own claim.

problemText: Galileo was tried in Rome in 1633, forced to recant publicly, and kept under house arrest until his death in 1642. Yet support for the Sun-centered model kept growing across Europe in those same years. Which factor best explains why silencing him failed to stop the idea?
choices: The church formally reversed its position within a year of the trial
Galileo escaped house arrest and continued publishing openly in Rome
Printed books carried the arguments and the underlying measurements to scholars in many countries who could check them for themselves
Newton had already published universal gravitation, which settled the question before the trial began
hints: A court can compel a person. Ask what it cannot compel, once the reasoning is already in circulation on paper.

problemText: A student writes: 'Copernicus proved the Earth orbits the Sun in 1543 by looking through a telescope, and the church later executed Galileo for agreeing with him.' Which response corrects both errors?
choices: Copernicus did use a telescope, but he published nothing in his lifetime, and Galileo was executed in 1642

Copernicus argued mainly from mathematical simplicity and had no telescope, since none was turned on the sky until about 1609; and Galileo was forced to recant and lived under house arrest until his death in 1642 rather than being executed
Copernicus built his model on Kepler's elliptical orbits, and Galileo was acquitted in 1633 and honored by the church
Copernicus proved his model with precise measurements he made himself, and Galileo was exiled from Europe and died in England
hints: Handle the two errors separately: first check whether the technology existed in 1543, then check what the 1633 sentence actually was.

problemText: Defenders of absolute monarchy in the 1600s, such as Bishop Jacques-Benigne Bossuet, argued for the theory of divine right. According to that theory, where does a monarch's authority come from?
choices: Directly from God, making the ruler answerable to God rather than to any human body
From a written agreement negotiated with an elected assembly
From a vote taken among the kingdom's leading nobles
From the consent of the merchants and landowners who pay the taxes
hints: The whole point of the theory was to place the ruler beyond appeal. Ask which choice leaves no human body able to judge the king.

problemText: Louis XIV governed the French provinces through intendants, officials dispatched from the royal court rather than drawn from the great local noble families. What was the main political effect of this practice?
choices: It gave provincial nobles a formal veto over royal decrees
It created an elected assembly in each province of France
It placed day-to-day provincial authority in the hands of men who owed their positions entirely to the crown
It ended the tax exemptions long enjoyed by the nobility and clergy
hints: Ask who could remove an intendant from his post, and what that dependence means for whose orders he follows.

problemText: The English Bill of Rights of 1689 barred the monarch from suspending laws, from levying taxes without Parliament's consent, and from keeping a standing army in peacetime without consent, and it required Parliament to meet regularly. What kind of government did this settlement establish?
choices: A republic, since the office of monarch was abolished
A constitutional monarchy, in which a real king still ruled but only inside legal limits
A democracy, since most adult men could now vote for Parliament
An absolute monarchy built on the French model
hints: Check two things separately: was there still a king in England after 1689, and how many people could vote for the body that limited him?

problemText: Jean-Baptiste Colbert, finance minister to Louis XIV, subsidized French manufacturing, taxed imported goods heavily, and worked to build up colonies and a merchant fleet so that France would export more than it imported. What was the underlying purpose of this program?
choices: To lower prices for French buyers by inviting foreign competition into the market
To free the crown from any need for tax revenue by abolishing customs duties
To hand economic policy over to the Estates-General for approval
To maximize the revenue flowing into the royal treasury, which paid for the court, the officials, and the armies
hints: Follow the money to its destination. Everything Louis built cost cash, and only one of these choices explains where the cash was meant to end up.

problemText: Peter the Great of Russia issued the Table of Ranks in 1722, which tied a nobleman's standing to the office he attained in state service rather than to his family's birth alone. How did this strengthen the ruler's authority?
choices: It made noble status depend on service that the ruler could grant or withhold
It abolished serfdom and gave Russian peasants legal freedom
It transferred the appointment of officials to an elected national assembly
It removed the army from the tsar's control and placed it under noble command
hints: Ask what changes about a nobleman's loyalty when his rank stops being something he inherits and starts being something he is given.

problemText: Louis XIV is routinely described as an absolute monarch. Yet provincial law courts delayed registering his edicts, the nobility and clergy kept their tax exemptions throughout his reign, and his treasury repeatedly ran dry. What do these facts best demonstrate?
choices: Louis XIV was in practice a constitutional monarch bound by a written charter like England's
France was in fact governed by an elected national assembly during his reign
Absolutism names the authority monarchs claimed and built machinery to pursue, not a total control any of them achieved
Louis XIV held noticeably less power over his kingdom than English monarchs of the same period held over theirs
hints: Separate the advertising from the operation: what the theory asserted versus what the state could actually enforce.
Notice that the intendants, the standing army, and Versailles were all tools for closing that gap. States do not build tools for problems they do not have.

problemText: In The Spirit of the Laws (1748), Montesquieu argued that political liberty survives only under a particular arrangement of governing power. What arrangement did he recommend?
choices: Power divided among separate branches able to check one another
Power concentrated in a single hereditary monarch answerable only to God
Power held by a state church that supervises the civil government
Power exercised directly by all adult citizens gathered in one assembly
hints: The phrase students usually attach to Montesquieu is 'separation of powers.' Ask what separation requires.

problemText: An eighteenth-century writer argues that government is not a gift handed by God to one family, but an agreement people enter into so that rights they already possess will be protected, and that the agreement may be revised when it fails to do its job. Which idea is being described?
choices: Divine right
The social contract
Mercantilism
The general will
hints: The key words are 'agreement' and 'may be revised.' Ask which term names government as a bargain rather than as an inheritance.

problemText: In The Wealth of Nations (1776), Adam Smith broke with the mercantilist economic thinking that had guided rulers such as Louis XIV. According to Smith, what makes a nation genuinely wealthy?
choices: Accumulating stocks of gold and silver while restricting imports
Royal ministers deciding which goods each province is permitted to produce
Conquering colonies and taxing their populations directly
Growing production and free exchange among people pursuing their own interests
hints: Three choices describe an economy steered from the top or measured by hoarded metal. Smith rejected exactly that.

problemText: An Italian writer argued in 1764 (paraphrased): 'Torture does not draw out the truth. It draws out whatever the sufferer believes will stop the pain, so that a strong-willed guilty man endures and goes free while a frail innocent one confesses and is condemned.' Which reform position does this argument support?
choices: Punishments should be made as severe as possible, since only fear prevents crime
Confessions obtained under torture are the most reliable evidence a court can obtain
Torture should be abolished because it produces unreliable evidence as well as needless cruelty
Punishment should be scaled to the social rank of the accused person
hints: The writer is making a practical claim before a moral one. Ask what he says torture actually produces, and whether that is useful to a court.

problemText: Rousseau argued that sovereignty belongs to the people as a whole, expressed through what he called the general will. Why did this claim threaten divine-right monarchy?
choices: It required every new law to be approved by the nobility and the clergy
It moved political authority from the state to the church
It held that monarchy is the only form of government capable of expressing the public good
It located the ultimate source of legitimate authority in the people rather than in a ruler chosen by God
hints: Divine right answers the question 'who is the source of authority?' Ask what answer Rousseau puts in that same slot.

problemText: A student writes that the Enlightenment thinkers formed a single unified movement demanding democracy and equal rights for everyone. Which response corrects this most accurately?
choices: They argued constantly among themselves and most were not democrats: Voltaire preferred a strong reforming monarch to rule by an uneducated public, Locke's framework suited a monarchy limited by consent rather than universal voting, and most of them assumed rights belonged to propertied European men
They agreed on democracy but were prevented from saying so openly by censorship
They rejected reason as a guide to politics and defended inherited custom instead
They were united in demanding the immediate abolition of slavery throughout the colonies
hints: Test the claim in two parts: did these writers agree with one another, and who did their word 'everyone' actually cover?

Recall that Mary Wollstonecraft had to argue in 1792 that women were included, and that enslaved revolutionaries had to take the language literally by force. Neither would have been necessary if the philosophes had already meant everyone.

problemText: In August 1789, France's National Assembly issued a document proclaiming that men are born free and equal in rights and that sovereignty rests with the nation. What was this document called?
choices: The Napoleonic Code
The Declaration of the Rights of Man and of the Citizen
The English Bill of Rights
The Edict of Nantes
hints: Two of these are not French at all or belong to a different century. Start by eliminating on date and country.

problemText: Colonists in British America answered the Stamp Act and the Townshend duties with the slogan 'no taxation without representation.' What was the core of that objection?
choices: That the rates being charged were higher than those paid by people living in Britain
That the colonies had been demanding full independence from the very start of the dispute
That Parliament, a body in which the colonies elected no members, had no rightful authority to tax them
That the taxes should be collected by the king personally rather than by Parliament
hints: Read the slogan literally. It names a missing condition, not a price that is too high.

problemText: In Spanish America, wealthy colonists of Spanish descent who had been born in the Americas were often rich and locally powerful, yet the highest colonial offices were reserved for officials born in Spain. What term names this American-born group?
choices: Creoles
Peninsulares
Philosophes
Intendants
hints: One of the other terms names the Spain-born officials who held the offices these colonists were denied. Keep the two groups straight by birthplace.

problemText: France entered the American war in 1778 to weaken Britain, and Britain conceded American independence in 1783. Historians often call this a strategic success and a financial disaster for France. What best explains the second half of that judgment?
choices: Britain seized and occupied French territory in Europe as compensation for its loss
The fighting destroyed French farmland and workshops on a large scale
France was required by treaty to pay reparations to the new United States
The loans and campaigns piled fresh debt onto a treasury already strained, under a tax system that largely exempted the nobility and clergy
hints: Ask where the war was actually fought, then ask who in France was legally obliged to pay for it.

problemText: In 1802 Napoleon moved to restore slavery in France's Caribbean colonies and sent an expedition to enforce that policy in Saint-Domingue. How did this decision shape what happened there?
choices: It convinced the formerly enslaved population that only full independence could secure their freedom, and they declared it on January 1, 1804
It persuaded the colony to accept continued French rule in exchange for trade privileges
It changed nothing, because Saint-Domingue had already been an independent state since 1791
It led Britain to conquer the colony and annex it to its own empire
hints: Ask what remaining part of France means once France has announced it intends to re-enslave you.

problemText: Both the Haitian Revolution and the Spanish American independence movements ended European colonial rule. Yet Haiti destroyed the social order of its colony, while most new Spanish American republics of the 1820s left racial and class hierarchies substantially in place. Which difference best explains that contrast?
choices: Spain granted its colonies independence peacefully, while France fought a long war to keep Saint-Domingue
Haiti's revolutionaries rejected Enlightenment arguments, while Spanish American leaders built their movements on them
In Haiti the revolution was made by the enslaved themselves, while in Spanish America it was led by creole elites whose grievance was exclusion from high office rather than the hierarchy below them
Slavery and racial hierarchy had already been abolished across Spanish America well before independence, so there was nothing left to change
hints: Start with who led each movement and what each set of leaders personally stood to gain once the European power was gone.
A revolution tends to remake exactly what its leaders were injured by. Ask whether the injury was a ceiling above one group or the whole structure.
